newsitem.title: USA: Mortgage-backed prices falter in wake of Greenspan.
newsitem.headline: Mortgage-backed prices falter in wake of Greenspan.

text.p: Mortgage-backed securities (MBS) ended slightly lower Wednesday after Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan concluded his Humphrey Hawkins testimony with remarks that left the capital markets expecting steady monetary policy in the near-term.
Some market participants reported movement out of MBS into Treasuries amid fears that more mortgage holders might refinance their loans amid lower rates.
Late in the session, discount mortgage coupon prices were off as much as 6/32, while premium coupons were off as much as 3/32.
One New York trader said that MBS "took it on the chin" earlier in the session, but later declines in Treasuries helped narrow spreads to Treasuries.
Mortgages improved marginally as Treasury prices declined, a New York pass through trader said.

One New York market participant contended that MBS remained little changed late in the session and said an investor moved from Federal National Mortgage Association (FNMA) 8.0-percent coupons into Government National Mortgage Association 8-percent coupons.
"The investor may have been extending duration," the market observer said.

Late in the session, GNMA 7.5 percent coupons were off 2/32 at 101 17/32 to offer a bond equivalent yield of 7.301. FNMA 7.5 percent coupons were off 4/32 at 101 11/32 and Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp 7.5 percent coupons were off 6/32 at 101 16/32.
Meanwhile, the Treasury's 10-year note was off 6/32 at 103 14/32 to yield 6.15.
Players said the MBS market would be sure to pay close attention to the Mortgage Bankers Association's weekly refinance index to be released Thursday.
The weekly survey of mortgage bankers by the trade group has found that refinancings have risen in recent weeks as Treasury rates decline.

"People are expecting refinancings to increase. The purchase side (of the data) is interesting because it is another gauge of consumer demand," said Trenton Fletcher, a manager of a $1 billion mortgage portfolio for Key Asset Management.

One buysider said that while there was some movement out of mortgages into Treasuries, he does not expect to see a mass exodus out of mortgages. Much of that, the investor conceded, hinges on whether interest rates stay at current levels.
"Mortgages have generally held in quite well ... the (MBS) market remains vulnerable to economic news" that bode well for Treasuries, he said.
